# Conceptual foundations

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Definition of model fitting

Choose the parameters [$\theta = (\beta, \gamma)$]{style="color: steelblue;"} so that the model's output is [as close as possible]{style="color: tomato;"} to the data [$\mathbf{y}$]{style="color: steelblue;"}

- Everything depends on what we mean by *close*
- Whatever we decide, we write it as a number: an [objective function]{style="color: tomato;"} [$\mathcal{L}(\theta, \mathbf{y})$]{style="color: steelblue;"} that is small when the curve is near the data and large when it is far away
- Fitting then means searching over [$\theta$]{style="color: steelblue;"} for the values that make that number small

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Two formulations of the fitting problem

### Point estimation

::: {style="color: steelblue;"}
$$\hat{\theta} = \arg\min_{\theta} \mathcal{L}(\theta, \mathbf{y})$$
:::

The next two sections use two different choices of [$\mathcal{L}$]{style="color: steelblue;"}, the [sum of squared errors]{style="color: tomato;"} and then the [negative log-likelihood]{style="color: tomato;"}

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Posterior distribution

A probability for *every* [$\theta$]{style="color: steelblue;"} given the data, rather than the one best value

::: {style="color: steelblue;"}
$$p(\theta \mid \mathbf{y})$$
:::

This is [Bayesian inference]{style="color: tomato;"}, and it is where the lecture ends up. The two answers share the [likelihood]{style="color: tomato;"}, which we build in section 4

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Sources of uncertainty {.smaller}

Even with the right [$\beta$]{style="color: steelblue;"} and [$\gamma$]{style="color: steelblue;"} the curve will not pass through every point. There are several reasons for the mismatch, and the lecture deals with each of them somewhere

| Source | In the flu data | Where we deal with it |
|:-----------|:-----------------------------------------------|:---------------------------------|
| Observation | Not every pupil in bed was infectious, or counted | The likelihood (4) |
| Parameter | Several $(\beta, \gamma)$ pairs fit almost as well | Confidence intervals (4), the posterior (6) |
| Model | No latent period; everyone mixes with everyone | Model comparison (4) |
| Process | Chance in who infected whom, day by day | Particle filtering (7) |

------------------------------------------------------------------------

:::

## Identifiability {.smaller}

[**The problem:**]{style="color: tomato;"} different parameter combinations can produce nearly the same curve

- A high [$\beta$]{style="color: steelblue;"} with a high [$\gamma$]{style="color: steelblue;"}: fast spread, quick recovery
- A low [$\beta$]{style="color: steelblue;"} with a low [$\gamma$]{style="color: steelblue;"}: slow spread, long infections
- Both can give a similar epidemic, because what the data pin down is mostly the ratio [$R_0 = \beta N / \gamma$]{style="color: steelblue;"}

We will meet this three times today: as a tilted valley in the least squares surface, as wide profile likelihoods, and as a tilted cloud of posterior samples

[**Remedy:**]{style="color: tomato;"} bring in what you already know, for instance a plausible infectious period for influenza. In the Bayesian section that is exactly what a [prior]{style="color: tomato;"} is

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Starting point: least squares

We start with the simplest objective function there is, the [sum of squared distances]{style="color: tomato;"} between the points and the curve
